utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'd like to raise something with the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've asked for the witness to the kept out shortly. I would ask that we just go into private session shortly as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat. Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Major Senkic. I hope you had a good rest last night. I only wish to warn you, since we both speak the same language, that we mind the interpreters and try not to overlap. Mr. Senkic, you are a Major, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You live in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 28th of January, 1962?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are married and father of two?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You matriculated from the secondary school in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nodded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And at present you work for the administration and mobilisation and structuring at the joint headquarters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your superior is Brigadier General Mr. Hamid Bahto; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone and pause before answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Two matters -- three matters. Major, would you please come closer to the microphone. The interpreters are finding it difficult to hear. And could you pause after counsel asks the question. Leave a pause for the interpreters to interpret and then answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And could you say yes or no when counsel asks a question rather than merely nodding a head, so that it goes down on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may also ask the usher just to move a little bit the ELMO, because I cannot see the witness. [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. Perhaps I was responsible because my questions also came too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your superior, Brigadier Hamid Bahto, judging by his name, he's a Muslim, is he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have any problems when working with him or with other Muslims working there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you ever had any problems of this kind before?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for your earlier duties, Major Senkic, in April 1992, you were appointed assistant commander of the municipality staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, for personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We shall not go into the municipality staffs because we shall come to that later. But in December 1992, you were employed in the same job, you were assistant commander for structuring and personnel affairs in the newly established Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That brigade was established in the very first days of December, 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite correct, or more exactly on the 5th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as of then, until then, there were no HVO brigades in Novi Travnik, were there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was a joint brigade of two municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was that the only case in Central Bosnia to have one brigade for two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I believe we shall agree that all the other municipalities in Central Bosnia at least invariably fell on the principle one municipality, one brigade, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we could seize the opportunity of your presence, Mr. Senkic, to ask you: In these proceedings, an emblem of strength was frequently mentioned that was used for the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'll explain what it is about but first I have to ask the usher to help.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D71/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Major Senkic, do you recognise this emblem?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: This is our official coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This is the coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Federal. This is a patch that we wear on our left shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The army of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean the uniform, the uniform of the army of the Federation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in the upper left, the green lily on the green, whose symbol is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: This symbol was worn by the members of the ABiH during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the one on the right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: This is the fundamental symbol that the HVO members wore in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in the current emblem of the federation, if I understand you well, both peoples which make part of the federation wear these symbols?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is an agreed, authorised emblem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what does this blue part mean?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It means an aspiration towards the united Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is seen below, the witness has just said, "This is our longing, our striving for the united or aspiration towards the united Europe," why are there ten stars then? Could the witness tell us why there are ten stars?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't draw this sign. I do not know who its author is. That is how we see it, but it's not official, at least we never heard any official explanation of this emblem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So it has nothing to do with the cantons, has it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Major Senkic, I'm sure we shall agree that this is an emblem which all the members of the federation army wear on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the same emblem is also used on all the official papers and all the letterheads?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And wherever there are some military insignia, the official ones, this is invariably the only coat of arms used in the army?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also tell us, do you remember as of when did this come into force?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly the date when the coat of arms was agreed, but after the organisation of the federal army, but I wouldn't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you place it perhaps sometime in the period following the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let us go back to Stjepan Tomasevic. I do not think there will be any objections to a leading question just to expedite matters. After Stjepan Tomasevic was established, you first worked -- you were first employed with personnel and organisation affairs. Then for about six weeks, you were an advisor for IPT, then you once again became the assistant commander for organisation and personnel and it was in that capacity that you saw the war end.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major Senkic, I should like to ask you to explain the system of mobilisation used in the former Yugoslavia, the concept of the mobilisation, that is, which was applied by all parties to the conflict in Bosnia and which was usually known under its acronym "PRAMOS"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Only briefly, PRAMOS means the rules of mobilisation of the armed forces and it was taken over from the system of the former JNA. As you have said, all the three sides used it and it was based on the following, I shall try to explain it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, perhaps it will be better if you did it step by step.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That system was applied to reserve units; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the concept in a nutshell meant that the army, the JNA, would be reinforced by reserve formations in case of need, that is in case of a war or threat of war; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you still apply that system in Bosnia, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Only slightly modified but this system is in force by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And during the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990, 1991, 1992, all three parties adopted the same system, did they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, so to speak, but I should like to dwell on --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: -- on the system of mobilisation in the HVO because we exchanged information with the others after that conflict and that is when I learned that they were using the same system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But within that concept, you called your brigade always with -- as R Brigade, R Brigades?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: R brigade or a war brigade meant that such formation is replenished from the reserve, that is fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. So in other words, that brigade is formed when there is a threat of war and it did not exist before except on paper?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, no, an order is issued to form it and their book of organisation is set up and then the R Brigade is formed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So such brigades never had any professional men?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That is why it was called R Brigade because it was replenished from the reserve exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there was also the so-called Territorial Defence, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was before the war. So the Territorial Defence existed before the war, and during the early days of the war it was extinguished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. A request put forth to the civilian authorities in municipalities, that is to say, to the secretariat of national defence, a request to assign a certain soldier of a certain speciality to the reserve brigade would come from the organisation of that brigade itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: In this case, I did that kind of work. I sent the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So let's be quite clear on this. In the brigade, you defined which soldier you needed with what kind of qualifications for which particular job?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: There already was the speciality that was -- that was part of the evidence records. As you know, in the former Yugoslavia, people served in the former JNA and then they received certain specialities while during their military service. So then when I would send this request, and when I said that I needed a certain speciality, a person with a certain speciality, then they would find a certain person in their records and send me such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This shows that that mobilisation procedure of a certain soldier starts with you in the brigade because you define what kind of profile you need, and then it is the civilian authorities, because this is the municipal civilian office that finds this particular kind of specialised person then this person is mobilised by the civilian authorities and sent to the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and for a certain amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So an important part -- the most important part of the mobilisation process takes place within the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Senkic, you will agree that under the circumstances of that conflict in 1992 and 1993, this entire organisation of yours, the concept that you had, that you took over, ultimately was based, to a large extent, on improvisation and on the abilities of the persons who did the job; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this R Brigade was supposed to have a total of 2.864 members in an ideal situation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it was according to the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as regards its elementary set-up, it was supposed to have its staff, it was supposed to have a security platoon for securing the staff?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was supposed to have three infantry battalions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it was supposed to have certain specialised units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, attached to the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what these units attached to the staff are?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Engineering, signals, logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the concept that was used did not envisage a military police unit in the R Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However, as we mentioned earlier on, there was a platoon that was envisaged to take care of the security of the command post?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that platoon was supposed to be some kind of a guard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please -- I do apologise. I'm hurrying a bit. Tell me, you knew Mrs. Gordana Badrov, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: We did the same job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You did the same job while you were in Stjepan Tomasevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when the Viteska Brigade was established, you cooperated with it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: She worked in the Viteska Brigade, she did the same kind of job involving personnel as you did in Tomasevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that she had certain problems in that period of time when attempts were made to organise the brigade and that therefore she often came to you seeking papers, documents, books, and advice as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you did help her in this respect?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Through these contacts with Mrs. Badrov, could you see -- were you informed through that what the situation was concerning the Viteska Brigade on the day when the conflict broke out in the Lasva Valley, the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: In addition to these unofficial meetings with Mrs. Badrov, we also had regular official meetings of the heads for organisation and personnel, so we followed each other's situations. I knew that she had a lot of problems. I knew that she did not have the necessary documentation, that she was starting from scratch, and I tried to help her.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, you did have insight as far as the establishment of the Viteska Brigade was concerned from its very inception?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Once the war broke out I imagine you did not have such insight any longer.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You had these working meetings, as you mentioned. These were meetings within the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this was your joint command that was superior to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Within that framework at that time, that is to say, on the 7th of April, 1993, a seminar was held precisely for UKP, that is to say, for officers working on UKP?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were several. I mean, these meetings were held quite often. These were working meetings, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would we agree that actually at that time, the beginning of April, the question of the establishment and organisation of the HVO was looked into, and actually it was observed that HVO had certain problems in this regard, and generally speaking, the army could not have been satisfied with the existing state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: These problems were of a continuous nature. They were never fully defined. The organisational set-up was never completed and there weren't enough resources in order to carry this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a professional who is involved in such work until the present day, could you say, when you had your best period in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, which you knew very well, to what percentage, let's put it that way, were the objectives of the brigade met? Was it set up by 30 per cent or 70 per cent or 80 per cent, in the best period of time you had?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: You have to know that there is personnel and that there is materiel that has to be taken into account. In order to establish an R Brigade, in order to have all the necessary personnel, according to the systematisation from the book of establishment, and according to the materiel book of establishment, this was theoretically impossible, because there wasn't even a minimum of resources, and also the personnel structure was a very critical one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So all of these are elements that practically prevented you from reaching a solid level of establishment?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: At brigade level we did not have a single professional from the former JNA. All of these persons were either reservists, reserve officers, or volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that was the situation that prevailed in your brigade, in the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm talking about the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was the same, more or less, in all brigades in Central Bosnia; you weren't better or worse, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody had the same problems for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt that the Viteska Brigade and the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade were that type of brigade, R type?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: All brigades in Central Bosnia were R type of brigades, so all of them were fully replenished from the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you managed to establish them, to the extent to which you managed to establish them, according to the situation you had at hand, even though you lacked personnel?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please, let us go back to this short part about the establishment of the brigade and the military police, or generally speaking, the establishment of the HVO that you had in Central Bosnia. The military police -- now I'm talking about Central Bosnia in 1992 and 1993 -- was it subordinated to the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If the commander of the brigade or his officers was supposed to take a soldier who had not reported for duty, who did not go to the front line, who did not show up, whatever, how did the brigade resolve that? How was this person brought in?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, we sent the brigade command a request to bring in these soldiers who had not responded and who had thus committed a disciplinary infraction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a battalion. Which battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The 4th Battalion of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if a brigade needed a certain intervention of the military police for its needs, then it has to send a request to the command of the military police, which then carries out that particular task if that is within the domain of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any exception? Was there any case in which the brigade could have commanded the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The military police? In Novi Travnik there weren't any exceptions. In Novi Travnik no one commanded the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether that was ever the case in Vitez, to the extent to which you were familiar with this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, let us now move on to another subject. During 1992, while there was still the Municipal Staff and when the brigade was also set up, what were the only tasks of your HVO in Novi Travnik in the sense of military activities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The defence of the line against the Serbs, against the VRS. We called them the VRS, that is, the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You had certain sectors in the mountains to the north-west of Travnik that you held from Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These were sectors at the front line, and that is where you defended yourselves from VRS aggression; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You practically held those lines from the summer of 1992, I believe, until late in 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In which way, speaking from an organisational point of view, were these lines held? Which units were those lines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, these were the members of the R Brigade of Stjepan Tomasevic, the mobilised members of the R Brigade of Stjepan Tomasevic. We have to use this term, the R Brigade. We have to realise that this was a brigade entirely composed of reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So Stjepan Tomasevic is an R Brigade and it sends its soldiers to the front line; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How did it mobilise this unit? Let me ask you one thing before that. This brigade, Stjepan Tomasevic, this reserve brigade, Stjepan Tomasevic, it does not have barracks; it does not keep its troops in one place. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So when troops are needed, they have to be called up from home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the brigade headquarters decides that the front line has to be manned? And how is it actually carried out, then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: There is an operative assessment that has to be made in terms of how many soldiers are needed in order to hold the front line, the defence line, and on the basis of this operative plan, people are mobilised for defence. Then in this way the unit is manned and sent to the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that a theoretical model that we discussed at the very outset was then being applied?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So a certain number of soldiers are going to be called up?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And according to these call-up papers, they have to report at a certain place at a certain time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then, when they report, according to these call-up papers, to the brigade, then the brigade sends these persons, after having established a unit, to the defence line up in the hills; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then this person stays up there for 7 to 10 days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then this person returns?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the same time, another shift goes up there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the man who returned, if he is employed, for example, in the Bratstvo factory or somewhere else, he goes to work; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Who worked would go back to work, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if this person were a farmer in his village?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Then he would again be involved in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that moment when this person returns from the defence line to his village or town, is he still a soldier of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, not until he is called up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So he is on the list of persons who can be mobilised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, only that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We are being cautioned all the time. We should speak slower, because we don't want things to be missed from the transcript. This person remains on the list for mobilisation, on the basis of which mobilisation is carried out, but at this moment, when this person has completed his shift, his number of days up there, he is no longer a member of the brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell us, please: If such a soldier who has just come back from his shift commits a crime, kills his neighbour, is involved in a traffic accident, whatever, under whose jurisdiction is he then, criminal jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Such things happened, yes, they did happen, but that was under the jurisdiction of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what if that same soldier committed that crime while on the front line, up in the hills, against the army of Republika Srpska, and then flees from the front and commits a crime? Under whose jurisdiction is he then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Because he was in uniform, because he had been under call-up at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The BH army and the army of Bosnian Serbs used some facilities of the former JNA and had their troops stationed in barracks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, that is common knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But they also used the system of reserve brigades, as you did?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they have in the barracks billeted the troops from R Brigade or did they have a separate system, that is, where some were in the barracks and others were like yours, depending on mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the technology that they used and that was information that I received after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, just tell us in a couple of words.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander who had a way -- where to accommodate people kept his troops there, but those were no longer our brigades because that brigade would change its profile and then it would become a brigade of another type.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the Bosnian army had such brigades?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, manoeuvre brigades of different sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Hence since you mention it, the personnel structure, it was the general view that the BH army had a much higher, better structure, that is, that there were more officers amongst its ranks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is logical because they were more numerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there was no doubt that there was this difference between the HVO and the BH army regarding the officer corps, that that difference was quite striking?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it is to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But let us go back to -- no, excuse me, we forgot one thing. You just told us how the front line was manned in 1992, the front line against the ARS since the establishment and during the life of Stjepan Tomasevic, I mean the Brigade Stjepan Tomasevic, of course. But what happened a few months before that while the municipal staff was responsible for the organisation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly improvised but this -- these cycles went on. There were no formation books, it was improvised, that is, unit by unit, were called up to man the front line against the Serbs, that is ARS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is people were sent to the front on the basis of the same principle even though the organisation at the headquarters itself was different than in the subsequently established Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was set up on the 6th of December, 1992, and it was the joint brigade. Who was its first commander, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correction, 5th of December, 1992. The first commander was Boro Malbasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Malbasic didn't come from Novi Travnik, he came from outside, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] came from Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And his head, the head of his staff, that is, head of the Stjepan Tomasevic staff was Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Major Senkic, tell us, did you know Cerkez before that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So basically, that is when you met him, when he joined the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: At the first meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you were also a member of that staff, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We already said what you were responsible for. So you were a colleague of the accused Mario Cerkez in the staff which was headed by Borivoje Malbasic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid there was a slip in the transcript, but let us perhaps clarify it through a question. Malbasic came from Vares, not you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Malbasic, yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, because it needs to be corrected. And then later on in the beginning of February 1993, Malbasic was removed or rather sent to another duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is, he was sent back to Vares?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Whatever the case, you were sure that he quit the duty of the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade sometime in the early days of February, yes, February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As of that moment, did Mario Cerkez de facto take over the command of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to make it quite precise, you knew and you saw the document appointing Cerkez the acting commander, the representative of the commander?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that such a document, such powers of an acting commander, and that was the order of the superior command that that, in point of fact, meant "temporary" until the final decision was made, the acting commander was the first man in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. That is a temporary document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that to all intents and purposes, Mario Cerkez was now the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he remained in Novi Travnik with Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade until the beginning of March, 1993; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Stjepan Tomasevic, in that command while you were together, that is, while it was the joint command in February, March or rather December 1992 to March 1993, you were -- there was several officers from Vitez and from Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a combined command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in March 1993, when Cerkez left, other people from Novi Travnik also left Novi Travnik for Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before the departure, before the separation, Stjepan Tomasevic had two battalions; is that correct? It had two battalions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One battalion was replenished with men from Novi Travnik, that is conscripts from Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the other one with conscripts from Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, while Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was adjoined intramunicipal brigade, did it have any other tasks apart from fighting against the former JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs which, at that time, were aggressors in Bosnia-Herzegovina and constituted a special threat to the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: That was the only and exclusive task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Senkic, do you know of any case during that period of time, that is between December 1992 and March 1993, of any incident, of any conflict in which members of your brigade, Stjepan Tomasevic, would be involved?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that at that same time, it is true there were incidents here and there in the town, in the municipality, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: There were always incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But those incidents did not take -- but the brigade or the members of the brigade were not involved in those incidents either by accident or by order or apart from any order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In point of fact, at that time, in Novi Travnik, there was a truce, there was a cease-fire and there were no conflicts, armed conflicts between the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But we shall come back to that in greater detail. I shall come back to that later on. Before that, I should like to apologise to the Court and our learned friends because we omitted something from this summary. In 6.4 it says "Filipovic" but it should be "Totic" and since we are discussing errors, also, in paragraph 10, it says 93 Domobran Regiment and I think it should be 90th, but we shall ask the witness about that. Major Senkic, the last and significant incidents before the conflict in the valley at least in Vitez, and on that part of the valley on the 16th of April 1993, that such incident was the abduction of your officer and several men of his; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt that they were abducted by extremist Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was very serious action take in which there was a certain cooperation with the BH army to locate those men?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then two days later, there was also the brutal abduction of Zivko Totic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: We knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is you knew about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were told that at the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And while Cerkez was a member of the command under Malbasic, during Malbasic's time, did he have, as the chief of the staff, since there was no war, except for the front lines up there, did he have any special tasks, any priority tasks put to him by Malbasic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well we knew, we were -- in principle, we knew why Mr. Cerkez had been appointed, that is, there were problems regarding the relations between the command of our brigade and the civilian authorities. Mr. Cerkez came to put those relations right and to take care of the logistics, that is, of the brigade and to establish its functioning for the two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, did I understand you well, was he there to see to it that the municipalities begin to finance and equip the joint brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he had to mediate in the agreements between the two in the negotiations between the -- in the talks between the two municipalities regarding the [inaudible] brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you think he fulfilled that task?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that financing was underway?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And was your job specifically -- let us slow down, yes. And as far as your job was concerned, did you notice some improvement regarding coordination with civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And Cerkez had yet another task that was his second task, long-term task so to speak, given him by Malbasic. Do you remember what that was, what was the other area of his work?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Organisation of the front line, the engineering works, organisation of approach to front lines. That is front lines against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. Front lines against the Serbs. And did you -- were you aware in view of the daily briefings of the command, was there any progress in that area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what was -- who was Cerkez's first man in that regard, I mean the engineering works regarding the front lines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Colonel Zeljko Sabljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And Zeljko Sabljic who -- then succeed Cerkez when he left Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I should now like to move on to the topic of interethnic relations in Novi Travnik while Cerkez was there. We only touched upon that, perhaps we should explain it now. Major Senkic, the first interethnic conflict that you called noteworthy, a significant incident, when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the first incident in Novi Travnik between Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Until that time, there were no serious conflicts between those two peoples?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you say "never", you mean in history?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: In that particular area, yes. Even in history, there were none before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that situation as far as I understand it, was calmed down very quickly in a couple of days?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It was practically a one-day conflict; that is, everything was resolved in a matter of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is talks, politicians and so on and so forth and things calm down?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Without going into details, because I do not think it is particularly relevant, and when did then the next incident in Novi Travnik happen?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: In October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: That was sometime around the time that Jajce fell so it could be sometime around the 20th of October, and I think that that conflict lasted about five days, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this conflict was more serious than the one in June?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what was the practical consequence of that conflict in October after it calmed down?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It was when the resettlement, that is, the swapping of flats between two parts of the town took place. And a couple of months later, the town was, to all intents, divided, the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So a boundary, a demarcation line was set up so to speak and it became obvious which side controlled which part of the town?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So during this conflict in October 1992, there were some negotiations at a higher level?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was discussed at a higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is it true that that cease-fire, this partition of the town lasted until about the end of May, 1993 when the BH army attacked the mixed village of Senkovci?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Senkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Senkovici, I see. So we can see from that that since December 1992 until March 1993, that is while Cerkez was in Novi Travnik and member of the command, and the commander for a while, there were no conflicts between Muslims and Croats in any organised sense of the word. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no conflict between BH army, as an institution, as an organisation, on one side and the HVO on the other; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have any idea about the casualties at that part, that is to say, from December 1992 until March 1993, and about the incidents that occurred at that time? Was it only one people that suffered or were all victims?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: All were victims. All were victims but in Novi Travnik, it is a well-known fact that there were more victims among the Croats. I personally was a member of the commission for resolving incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to show a statistical map here. Let us have a look at the municipality of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this, Mr. Kovacic, you're going to show us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a statistical map showing the ethnic distribution of the population in the municipality of Novi Travnik or rather in these municipalities in Central Bosnia. We are particularly interested in the municipality of Novi Travnik only, that is, in the middle of this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where does this document come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It comes from the system that the Federation uses nowadays. It is used by the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia also. It is an integrated database. These are the only official data that are used nowadays in that area. They are based on the census that we have been using until now as well, that is to say, the census of 1991. I have only two questions in relation to this map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D72/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Senkic, could you please take a look at the monitor. Can you see this map? And please use this pointer to show the Trial Chamber the boundaries of the municipality of Novi Travnik. You will be assisted by the usher. Could we please zoom in on this.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. So this is the municipality of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Next to it is the municipality of Vitez. Could you please show that now.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: So this is the municipality of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then up here is the municipality of Travnik; is that correct? Economically this was always a single entity, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: People lived in one municipality, worked in another, commuted on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just to give a better idea of all of this, we are now only talking about the administrative boundaries of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in order to get a better idea of this, in peacetime, in order to go by car from Vitez to Novi Travnik, and further on to Travnik, how many minutes are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Fifteen to twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Just to give the Trial Chamber a better idea. As for the municipality of Travnik, in this pocket around Novi Travnik there is a red line. Can you explain what it denotes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: That is the defence line, the defence line, towards the BH army forces in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After which conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: After the outbreak of the war; that is to say, in the month of May, or rather June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So after the first conflict between the Muslims and the Croats in the municipality of Novi Travnik, after the month of June 1993, this is the line that was practically established, and that is the way it remained throughout the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the Croats remained in this upper north-eastern part of the municipality, and all the rest of the municipality was under BH army control?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We can remove the map, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Senkic, you were an officer in the HVO from the very inception of the brigade and until peace was established, until after the Washington Accords. Were you ever witness to or an agent of a policy of an officially organised persecution of Muslims in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anybody ever say to you that the HVO wished to achieve the displacement of the Muslim population from the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No. No. When the HVO was established, we worked together, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you that unofficially or secretly? Was there any kind of tacit conspiracy among the officers of the HVO that pressure had to be brought to bear against the Muslims so that they would move out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever do anything like that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No. Our only objective was to oppose, resist the VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The interpreter could not follow Mr. Kovacic's question. It was too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After this broader conflict broke out between these two ethnic groups, after April 1993, do you know what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, then we were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This policy was not changed in the sense of that somebody had to be persecuted, that civilians had to be persecuted, with the purpose of their leaving?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No. That was not the policy. The policy was defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that during 1993, after the conflict broke out in April, that military units on both sides took part in the conflict, that is to say, the military units of the BH army and the military units of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Basically?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While you held the lines against the Serbs, the BH army also in this sector -- Slatka Vode, Kamenjas, et cetera -- the BH army also held some sectors up there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you coordinate defence in these areas, at these lines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, this was done at the level of commanders and operations officers, so I am not quite familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But in principle this was agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have to be careful not to overlap each other. You answer immediately, even before I finish putting my question. We have to wait. So at the level of command everyone had to define this: who, up to where?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was the minimum of cooperation that had to exist; right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this cooperation continued even during the time that we mentioned, when, for example, your officers were abducted, when Zivko Totic was abducted?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At this time, when Mario Cerkez was in Stjepan Tomasevic, the commander of the BH army brigade in Novi Travnik was Beslim Zurapi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Bislim Zurapi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, Bislim Zurapi. Is it correct that cooperation between the two armies was at that time actually fair because there were fair officers on both sides?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct. But Mr. Cerkez was also on good terms, privately speaking, with some officers from the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You believe that this private relationship of his with his colleagues who were ethnic Muslims helped resolve matters more quickly?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes. By all means, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I understood this correctly, Bislim Zurapi, who was mentioned, was not an extremist; he was also a constructive and positive person in terms of these relationships?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of April 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back because of the transcript now. You said that Bislim Zurapi was positive; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what my experience was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a mistake in the transcript -- thank you -- so I had to put this question to you again. But now let's go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Basically, throughout the month of May, more or less, you were a member of the commission for resolving incidents in Novi Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you also had some better insight through this because you were a member of the commission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, while you were a member of the commission, since all were victims, which people were -- unfortunately, we have to say this statistically -- I mean, there were more victims coming from which ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time there was more pressure against the Croats in mixed villages, and as a member of the commission, we most often went to those areas. There were also persons who were killed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And looking at figures, were there more casualties among the Bosnian Croats or the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Among the Croats there were more victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that is at the time when you were a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the commission practically until the conflict itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you mention the names of these mixed villages, please, at least the main ones. There were always the main problem, where most Croat victims were.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Senkovci, then Torine, Rat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All of these villages are to the north-east of Novi Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: These are villages where there were incidents that were registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, if I may suggest that we go on the usual break just five minutes before, because after the break I would just go briefly through two documents which I should better prepare in order not to waste too much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Help me with one thing. It wasn't clear, Major Senkic, from your answer. It wasn't your fault. The question wasn't clear. You were asked about how long it took in a car, under normal conditions, from Vitez to Novi Travnik, and the question was rather confused because it went on to refer to Travnik. Your answer was "15 to 20 minutes." Now, is that the time that it would take in a car between Vitez and Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The distance is the same from Vitez to Novi Travnik and from Vitez to Travnik. If you look at the map there, you will see that the distance is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: My question is: How long does it take in a car between Vitez and Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. We'll adjourn now for half an hour. Could you remember, Major Senkic, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until its over and don't let anybody speak to you about it, and that does include the members of the Defence team. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've just reached paragraph 9 or rather 9.1 in our summary. Could we show the witness Z505, this is one of the lists, it is Tab 12 from this so-called Spork binder. Witness Senkic, will you please have a look at it and I will ask the usher to put it on the ELMO to see what list it is.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have to give him a Croatian copy. We gave him English. There are both. Probably the English should be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major Senkic, you saw that document, did you? Did you see this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was my service which made it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It has the date here, 27th of February, 1993, if I am correct.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you accept that this document was done by your service which means Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade on the 27th of February.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And from the manner in which it was stamped, I should say that it was done on a computer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So these records were stored in a computer?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, Cerkez commanded the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade, did he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 2nd Battalion which is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Anto Bertovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean Anto Bertovic from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, will you agree that the commander of the battalion -- for the record only, so Anto Bertovic was the commander of the 2nd Battalion, was he?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Will you agree that the battalion commander is mentioned nowhere in this list; that is, when you went through the list before, you did not see his name?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court what does this list mean, how was it compounded?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: This list is a list of soldiers engaged during the last month, that is soldiers engaged in military tasks. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So all these soldiers who, in January 1993, were on the front line, that is called up and sent to the front?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Or dealing with communications or engineering tasks, but all those who were engaged for various military tasks during the preceding month mostly on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you prepared such reports for every month, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, practically, until the break out of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it means that I cannot really establish with certainty on the basis of this list -- no, let me rephrase it. It means that I cannot see from this list how many soldiers were engaged in March, say? For that you would need the list for March, which was drawn up a month later?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: In April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me just one more thing. This report regarding the state in January, it seems to show that some 433 soldiers, if I count them correctly, were active, that is, were assigned various tasks in January; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in the preceding month and the month before that or a month later, that number could have been larger or smaller; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember what would be the order of magnitude, that is, between how many and how many roughly?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Plus/minus 15. I should say depending on the response of the soldiers that were called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We can then remove the list. Only for the record, the witness said, "Plus/minus 15 per cent". And will you please show the witness the second list from the same binder, Z332.1. Witness Senkic, there is no need to go through it, you can just look at the first two or three pages and the title page. I showed you this list before, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik, did you compile an identical document?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, my service drew up an identical document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we have the first page on the ELMO, please, only the first page for identification. If you now look at the top of the first page, not the one which is on the ELMO but the one which you have on the desk this list was drawn up for which units, it says up there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: This was for 92nd Domobran Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what was this regiment, which area did it cover whose was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It was the legal successor to the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it a legal successor to the Vitez Brigade only or did it also incorporate some other units which did not have their own legal successors?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The Domobran Regiment, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: I shall speak about Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us what was the state of affairs in Novi Travnik you were there so let us explain to the Court. In Novi Travnik after the war, the legal successor to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was also the Domobran Regiment, which number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Or was it 90th or the 93rd?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Or perhaps 90th or the 90th or the 93rd. No, the 90th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. But it was also called the Domobran Regiment, Home Guard Regiment, and it was the legal successor, you already told us, of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in your case in Novi Travnik, in that Home Guard regiment, was this regiment the legal successor to any other unit?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And its roster, did it include some other soldiers, soldiers who no longer had their basic units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: These lists include all who were in any way during the war against the BH army, who were involved, engaged, in any way whatsoever. So therefore not only the members of the former brigade, but also the civil defence and even civilians who were helping with logistics in any way: women, children who carried water, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Am I getting your meaning, that this roster includes all the persons from a particular territory -- we're referring to the territory of Vitez at this moment -- every individual who in any way whatsoever helped, contributed, to a defence of the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we just put some examples, such as, for instance: If a civilian had a house 500 metres from the front line, and if food was prepared for the platoon which was on the front line there, would such a person be included in such a roster?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if that person was a woman alone in that household, would she be put on the list?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And why were those lists compiled?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, a little before that, the BH army did that, that is, they made those lists for distribution of shares, of certificates, basically, so as to distribute the certificates. So they did it before us, on the basis of information that they also included individuals who were engaged with the army, about the army, around the army, in the army, in any way whatsoever, and that they put them on those books, on the record, so we did the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You say "certificates." What is that about? Will you please explain to the Court what are the certificates?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, all individuals, that is, all the individuals engaged in the defence, would be recognised the amount of salary, totalling 400 convertible marks, but in certificates, which now can be invested in privatisation funds and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean for the time spent in the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, for the time spent in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, every citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of what side he participated on in the Muslim Croat conflict, I mean, and even fighting against the Serbs, every citizen who participated in the war and in one way or another contributed to the war or the defence in that war, received some kind of compensation, of remuneration, from the state?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: From the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. From the Federation. You just explained that the certificates means that the state simply does not have money to pay the salaries for that period of time, so that it offered certain valuables, papers of value, so that these people could either buy flats or buy shares in enterprises, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that by compiling these -- that the compilation of these lists helped to contribute to the distribution of state funds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it really would be better if you'd let the witness give the evidence. These may well be matters which are very much in dispute. The witness should be simply asked an open-ended question: What was the purpose of compiling the lists? Now, you destroy the worth of the evidence if on matters of this sort you start giving the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will not lead on that. I thought it was more or less under no dispute, because it is commonly known knowledge in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, not here, and it may well be in dispute. Is there any dispute about this, Mr. Nice, as to why these lists were made up?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Hearing this evidence, I shall have to take some further instructions and give thought to the matter over the luncheon adjournment. I've already got it in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anyway, let the witness tell us about why these lists were compiled. Can you tell us, Major Senkic, why these lists were compiled?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: We were issued the order from the relevant command to compile lists, to make records of individuals, not only members of the brigade, but all persons who were engaged in the defence in one way or the other. And the purpose was to make a record so that these people could get bonds, or rather certificates, which the citizens could then later on use in the privatisation by investing in privatisation funds, purchase of shares, or purchase of other socially owned property. This process is under way in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes. The certificates were also issued for labour obligation; that is, people who worked for the Bratstvo factory in Novi Travnik before the war were also issued the certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness Senkic, do you know if it was done in all the other regiments, in adjacent municipalities and throughout Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: It was done in both components of the Federation army; that is, both the HVO and the BH army did that, except that the BH army embarked upon it a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But both components of the army, that is, both the Bosniak and the Croat one, applied the same criteria, didn't they, regarding this broad approach?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in the meantime, did you get those bonds or those certificates in the way which you could get the bonds?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just one more question bearing on that particular matter. If, to exercise any other right regarding disability or any of the property rights, a former soldier, either of the BH army or the HVO, needs a document to prove that he served in the armed forces, would an excerpt from such a list be enough for whatever administrative procedure?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
