utterances.text: All right. So then we can even find out from there that a person -- this person was born in that region?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I can't remember what these regions were called. Before I think this was Zenica. Well, never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you now please look at the amount of paper I've got up, it's about half of this document. This is the page where there are numbers 2686, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Is this compiled the same way?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we should have a look. On the top, on the top it says page 64. No, I think these are our own markings the ones that we put in ourselves, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, no, it's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the best thing would be if I gave the witness my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point that you want, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The point is -- excuse me, I will continue in Croatian. [Interpretation] The point is that the witness was asked a question that he could not have answered because he never saw this list before. He made the same kind of list in Novi Travnik though. The suggestion made was that there were only citizens there but my suggestion is that there are children here and I can prove this easily. There are children who are 14 and 15 years old and there are two of them on this page. I found another one who is 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We've heard the witness say that the relevant numbers include, in one column, the date of birth and with that in mind, it should be possible to work out your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we have finished with this, I thank you. At one point in response to the Prosecutor's question, you explained the relationship between the brigade commander and the civilian authorities in town. What did you exactly mean by "civilian authorities in town"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Civilian authorities function throughout the war. There was the head of the municipality, there were the heads of various departments, I don't know, in charge of economic affairs, defence, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The commander of a brigade in some municipality, in Novi Travnik, or Vitez, any municipality, the model is the same, really, I'm just asking whether you know. Why does he have to communicate and how with the civilian authorities in town?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, in the sense of logistic support. Because these brigades primarily relied upon what they were given by the municipality. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The pre-war concept that we discussed in the beginning that you explained and our brigade was always financed by its municipality, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then this president of the municipality, can he issue a military order to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: He cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he can decide about resources, about money?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, how much he can give us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just explain something here so that it would not remain unclear. You said explicitly, in response to the Prosecutor's question, that Novi Travnik was not on the communication line to Central Bosnia but it was Central Bosnia. So we agree that Novi Travnik is not on some kind of a highway going through Bosnia, going east, west, north, south, but it is close to these communication lines?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, on the contrary, it was not on these communication lines. Novi Travnik is actually a pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As for this main communication, Travnik/Vitez, Novi Travnik is about six kilometres away from the main communication line, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that military force which possibly seals off Novi Travnik does not, in that way, interrupt traffic along the main communication lines in that part of Bosnia, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no communications going through Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that area, the main communication line is the one that goes down Kiseljak, Busovaca, Vitez, Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: From Travnik onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Travnik onwards to Sarajevo, all possibilities are open?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the other side as well from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is the main road in this area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the main road in this area until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that is the road that Vitez is on, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There was no audible answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also said that every citizen had to have a pass in order to leave the territory of the municipality. First of all, is it correct that every citizen had to have a pass in order to leave the municipality during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, every military conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is to say that only a military conscript had to have a pass?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, only a military conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that's the way it was according to the regulations of the former Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was not envisaged. There were no such cases in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Of course. But the regulations envisaged that in a state of war, that measure could be imposed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, there would have to be special passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is to say that women and children could move about freely; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who were military conscripts, people of what age?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: From 18 to 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So a person who was younger than the age of 18 or over the age of 60 could move about without a pass?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, the events concerning the 20th of October, 1992 in Novi Travnik were mentioned. Do you remember whether, in these events, where there was a conflict, that the chief of the municipal staff, Mr. Ivica Stojak was killed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he was killed at a checkpoint that was under BH army control in Travnik, right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regardless of these incidents that occurred in the period from December 1992 until March 1993, was there any conflict between the units, even the smallest units or the biggest unit that belonged to the BH army or the HVO in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: There were no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The photocopy of this HVO ID of a soldier where the 1st Viteska Brigade is mentioned, a person by the name of Zoran Kristo, Z165/2, you noticed that it says municipal staff here on this seal. Tell me, when Stjepan Tomasevic, when the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade was established, was a seal made for the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Soon after the establishment of the brigade, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, that is procedure. One gets a seal very fast. I can't remember the date but it's very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you see that the Viteska Brigade in Vitez also had a seal?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In our parts, generally speaking, do people set great store by seals and stamps and if a document is only signed but not stamped, is it always a bit suspicious?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's right. Until the present day, our people tend to believe in seals. Even until the present day in the army of the Federation, people use seals and stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this confidence in a piece of paper with a seal, is this valid only in the military or in life in general in the area where you live?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, generally speaking, life in general. Nobody considers a document to be valid unless it's stamped.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear, in view of the neighbouring municipalities, that in the early summer, already from the month of May onwards, that there was an initiative and even an agreement reached in Vitez to establish a joint Muslim/Croat brigade which was even supposed to be called the HMVO; have you ever heard of that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it. I heard about this HMVO, about this name. I just heard about it, but I was not involved in this procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You do not know about the details?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So did you hear the term the 1st Viteska Brigade in regard to that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: The 1st Viteska Brigade? The 1st Viteska Brigade? That is a very arbitrary term. I know, because at that time, as staff, we cooperated. They wanted to have a formation. They wanted to have some kind of a name. For us, it was sufficient if it said municipal staff or the 1st Company or the escort company, so we -- we were -- we did not really have any hang-ups of this nature. We didn't have to be a formation. However, the men of Vitez, they wanted to be established in this way in some kind of a formation which actually was not a formation. They were a municipal staff, they cannot be a municipal staff -- there cannot be a brigade if there is a municipal staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The translation had not finished. Now, I'm looking at the clock. We want to start another witness. You've examined this witness for an hour and a half this morning, Mr. Kovacic. I really can't think there's very much more to add. He's been giving evidence all day. It's a question of whether it's really much assistance to the Tribunal of going over all these facts again when there's another witness waiting to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am really trying to cover only those matters which were raised in a different way during the cross-examination, and I merely wanted to touch upon some of the documents which the Defence has never laid its eyes on before. We do not challenge those documents in principle because we do have to accept them with reservation because we have not seen them before. And, as far as I know, the witness does not know anything about them. So I want to change that, and that is the only thing I wanted to address yet, and I won't go back to those matters that were already addressed, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Jokeris were mentioned, and an attempt is made to establish that they were in Travnik as of October 1992. Major Senkic, do you know when the Jokeris were established?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: I don't. Those members who were from Busovaca we called them Busovacans, those from Vitez, the Vitezans. I really don't know when the Jokeris were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there is a small undefined part in the question which has remained there so I have to ask you this: Is it possible that the Jokeris or the Vitezovi mentioned in that part of the transcript, in that part of the question were under Mario Cerkez's command?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez commanded the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, not at that time, thank you. Mario Cerkez's predecessor, Borivoje Malbasic, while he was the commander, could it be that he commanded a unit called Bruno Busic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him issue orders to it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Nobody could issue orders to them. I know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, nobody has suggested that Malbasic commanded the Bruno Busic Brigade. There is no need to go over evidence which hasn't been disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I had the impression that that was implied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, have we ever suggested that Malbasic commanded the Busic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To be fair I was making observations about the presence of outside HVO troops in the commander's territory, but I didn't go very far in that allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The document about mobilisation which mentions six hours for mobilisation, it is, all told, just a model, just a theoretical concept of mobilisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Which was done by an incompetent person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was also talk about the document entitled request and we were shown a specimen addressed to the military police from the brigade. Let us just clarify the force of that request. Is it true that the brigade can send such a request to the military police only for common activities of military police such as bringing in recruits who refused to report or failed to report; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is request only for the common military police duties, that is to bring in soldiers or perhaps if they caused disorders somewhere then of course the police could be called in to bring them in again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can a brigade commander send a request to the military police for it to go and join the combat somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Novi Travnik, a commander of the military police was somebody called Stipe Bavraka; is that true?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And tell me, if, in February 1993, if Cerkez had sent an order or even a request to that military policeman, Stipe Bavraka, what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Nobody could command Stipe Bavraka. One could talk to him, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that specific military policeman in Novi Travnik would not have obeyed him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Well, it would depend on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just two more questions, I did not want to go into it, but it seems that it was put to you towards the end. Major Senkic, you spent your youth in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Both my childhood and my youth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that is where you began your professional career?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness nods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is where you spent your career?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You spent the war there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you consider that place your homeland?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Has it ever occurred to you to leave it when the conflict between Muslims and Croats broke out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO SENKIC
utterances.text: Not then and not before that. At the time, we were -- when we were setting up the municipal staff, we were doing it to rid the Serbs because at that time we were in jeopardy. We were threatened by the Serb aggression. It certainly crossed nobody's mind, I don't know, but nobody thought -- nobody thought about the war between Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for coming, Major Senkic, to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. It is now concluded. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While we're changing witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have the new witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 1396 hadn't been produced already. I will arrange for enough copies to be available and distributed, 1396, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witnesses are being changed, Mr. Nice raised the prospect of certain motions or certain applications being brought before the Court. I have previously alerted him and Ms. Featherstone that I will be out of the country for the next week, back on August 1st. Could I ask that any argument scheduled or on those motions be scheduled for after August 1st?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, we have to rise at five past 4.00, so if you could find a convenient moment about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Cerkez's defence, I will ask you some questions. I will ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I am at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And I should also like to ask you to bear in mind that our conversation is being interpreted into the official languages of the Tribunal, and so will you please make a break between my question and your answer in order to facilitate the work and our court reporters. Mr. Peric, you were born on the 3rd of January, 1953, in Travnik; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are married, you are a father of five, of whom four sons and one daughter?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a teacher of physics and mathematics?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak up or come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And it was in Rijeka where you were educated?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Rijeka is a town, is a port in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After you graduated from the teacher's faculty, you served your military service with the JNA in Kragujevac, in the Republic of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did you undergo any specialisation in the army, or perhaps did you get the rank?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I became a lance corporal. During that first year, students came for their military training, and since I was a university graduate, I delivered lectures to them. And to be able to deliver lectures, I needed a rank, and that is how they gave me the rank. But I never went to any training to become a lance corporal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when was it that you served the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It was during my studies, that is, after my second year of studies. At that time you could serve only one year, that is, 12 months, so I benefited from that and I made a break in my studies. It was in 1974, in the autumn of 1974 that I left, did my army service, and then I came out of the army in August, the next year, and went on with my studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Before those unfortunate events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, former Yugoslavia, you lived and worked in Varazdin, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Varazdin is also a town in the Republic of Croatia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the north of Croatia. It used to be a capital once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you taught physics and mathematics in a secondary school, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At the moment you live in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are a businessman and you are engaged in commerce?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, when the war broke out in the Republic of Croatia in 1991, you were teaching at the secondary school in Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you wanted to report as a volunteer in that conflict, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was a conflict, in point of fact, between the JNA and nascent armed forces of the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But they did not accept you as a volunteer at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was the reason for refusing to take you in?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That it was my labour obligation to work in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you had your working hours, you were employed by the school and at the school, and during your leisure hours you self-organised, in a way, to follow the events in the town. What is it that you did?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the national protection detachments. That is what they were called. And they were voluntary. It was in neighbourhood communities or boroughs within the town. I have a flat at the Banfica in the town of Varazdin, and that is where we organised it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The principal role of these self-organised groups was to monitor the army, was to keep an eye on the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, because Banfica is a new part of Varazdin and it is where the officers and NCOs of the JNA live. And our task was to keep an eye on them and prevent them from leaving their apartments and getting to the barracks in case of a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But formally speaking, you were not members of armed forces or armed unit of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Of the HVO -- you mean HV? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the war in Croatia escalated, and in the summer of 1992, when the school year ended, you set off to your native land, that is, to the area of Novi Travnik in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: I went because the war had begun in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serbs attacked the areas of Central Bosnia, where the majority of the population was made of Muslims and Croats, and I went to help there because I have relations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which ones of your relatives were in the area of Novi Travnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Then, and now, all my relations -- three brothers, three sisters, my parents -- meanwhile my mother died -- and their children, so all my relatives, my whole family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time you also had a house in the village of Stojkovici?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Peric, tell us: That house in Stojkovici, what part of Novi Travnik municipality is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It is next to the former sports airfield in Stojkovici, on the Travnik-Novi Travnik road. That is about two or three kilometres, as the crow flies, from Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Before you therefore set off to help, to lend a hand in the defence of the village, you also obtained, procured for yourself a uniform and weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did that in 1991, at the time when the struggle for the independent state of Croatia began. Then I was involved in that and I made my contribution; that is, we who were for it, we were donating money for the purchase of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And this fund-raising was, in a manner, also organised by neighbourhood communities, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you, de facto, bought the uniform and the weapons?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And then you put that uniform and the weapons into your car and set off in the direction of Novi Travnik; is that so?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And when you arrived in the area of Novi Travnik, you reported to the HVO as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes. I reported in my village because my brothers were already included, and only a few days after I arrived, a shift from our village was to go to the feature at Kamenjas. And as soon as I arrived, it was agreed that all of us who were slightly older, that is, the generation of 52, 53, that we should go there together, just as a group, because we were all one company but still in school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. But who did you report exactly, as a volunteer, when you went back to your village in Stojkovici? I don't mean a person. I mean a body.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No. There was no special body for that. I simply heard from my brothers that the shift was to go within two or three days, and I said, "Well, then I'm coming along." That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So in point of fact, those were villagers who went into the mountain, to the front line against the Bosnian Serbs, that is, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how long did the shift stay on the front line?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: At that time -- well, basically it was seven days, but I immediately stayed two shifts in a row.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you would then do your shift and you would come back to your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And go about your daily, normal, regular business?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You already described to us how you came by your uniform and your weapons. And what about other people in the village? How did they obtain the uniforms and weapons, and did they have any?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, not very much of it, but they did have something. They had taken it -- I don't know exactly when, whether it was the spring or summer of that same year, 1992 -- from the barracks at Slimena. So some weapons came from there. And they also had some hunting rifles which were their own private property. And I believe they also bought some there, paying for them out of their own pocket. How, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the barracks at Slimena. Just to remind Their Honours, it is the former JNA barracks which the JNA had left and yet left some weaponry behind.

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then those weapons were distributed amongst the local population?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, therefore, summer/autumn 1992, there was an armed conflict under way between the JNA and the army of Bosnian Serbs, on the one hand, and the local population, Croats and Muslims, on the other. They were defending their area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in your native area?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: Well, until, I think, about mid-August, but then I had to report to the school on the 20th of August, so I don't know exactly when I left. But it must have been sometime in mid-August when I went back to Varazdin to resume my regular work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. So even though villagers held some parts of the front line, are you also aware that from a wider area, for instance, from Vitez, there were also shifts which helped to defend the territory against the aggression of the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: It was, when I was there -- well, I couldn't really tell you the exact number, but there must have been some 20 members from Vitez who were with us. The exact number, whether it was 19 -- but it was around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. And when you returned back to your job in Varazdin in the Republic of Croatia, did you leave your uniform, your weapons, in the village or did you take them back to Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: BOZO PERIC
utterances.text: No. I thought it was my property, because I'd paid for them, so I took them with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your Honours, perhaps this might be a convenient time for the break until tomorrow, because we are moving on to another paragraph, that is, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now. In fact, it will be till half past 11.00 tomorrow morning, because there is another case with which the Trial Chamber is occupied earlier. Mr. Peric, would you come back, please, tomorrow morning at half past 11.00 to continue your evidence. Meanwhile, would you remember not to speak to anybody about it, and that does include members of the Defence team, until your evidence is over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Eleven-thirty tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of July, 2000, at 11.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
